title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI systems were used to create fake interviews and articles impersonating real financial figures to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The fabricated content presented false endorsements as though they were real news stories, exploiting the credibility of established journalists and officials. Detection would have required either verification that the interviews actually occurred before sharing the articles, or examination of the underlying recordings and source material before publishing.

The deployment failure was not in the AI model itself but in the absence of authentication steps before scam content reached victims. Scammers used AI-generated or manipulated media as part of a larger fraud operation, embedding it in fake websites and advertisements designed to appear legitimate. What is not established is which specific AI tools or techniques created the deepfakes, or whether victims could have distinguished the fake content from genuine reporting without external verification.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated confrontation with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler never actually occurred. The fabricated story was designed to promote Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn people to avoid. This incident exemplifies a rising category of scams that use artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfake content featuring well-known Australians and politicians to trick people into investing money.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that investment scams have become increasingly sophisticated and prevalent. Last year, regulators removed 19,400 scams overall, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, along with other politicians and prominent financial figures like Alan Kohler, are frequently impersonated in these schemes. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fake websites, news articles, and advertisements to lure victims. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
